title: Forking Twice: A Nested Branch from Within a Branch

turns.userMessage: (Branch A) Before finalizing, let's fork again here to compare write-through vs write-back caching for the Redis layer.
turns.assistantResponse: Forking again from this point — I'll try write-through in one branch and write-back in the other.
turns.explanation: A second fork, this time from inside Branch A instead of from the original trunk. This nested fork point (cache size 6,100 = the original trunk plus everything Branch A added) is itself now a shared trunk for two new sub-branches (write-through vs write-back) — exactly the same mechanics as the first fork, just one level deeper. Both new sub-branches inherit this full 6,100-token history as a warm cache hit; nothing needs to be rebuilt, and Branch B (from turn 3) is completely unaffected.

turns.userMessage: (Branch A.1 — write-through) Implement the write-through variant.
turns.explanation: Branch A.1 reads the full 6,100-token nested trunk (original trunk + Branch A's own work + the second fork point) as a cache hit, then diverges with its own write-through-specific content. A parallel Branch A.2 (write-back, not shown) reads that identical nested trunk independently. Branch A.1's total on top of the nested trunk is about 0.0108 AI Credits; its full session cost (0.0289 + 0.0115 + 0.0109 + 0.0171 + 0.0107 + 0.0108 = 0.0899 AI Credits) reuses the original trunk once and the Branch-A-specific work once, rather than paying for either a second time. Running three entirely separate sessions for Branch B, Branch A.1, and Branch A.2 from scratch would instead pay for the trunk three times and Branch A's own work twice — nesting the fork compounds the savings further down the tree, not just at the first split.
